method: Each entry records how it was checked. 'Opened' means the page or document was retrieved from the publisher's own domain and the quoted words were read there. 'Official-domain search excerpt' means the words were read in a search result served from the publisher's domain, without opening the whole document. Nothing is marked verified beyond what the quoted words support.

irs_basis.title: Gifts and inheritances: is money from the sale of inherited property taxable?
verifies: Basis of inherited property is generally fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if elected on Form 706
Selling for more than that basis is a taxable gain, reported on Schedule D and Form 8949
irs_basis.quote: The fair market value (FMV) of the property on the date of the decedent's death (whether or not the executor of the estate files an estate tax return ...). ... If you sell the property for more than your basis, you have a taxable gain.
irs_basis.checked: opened on the publisher's site in this session

boe_prop19.title: Proposition 19: comparison charts, questions and answers, filing checklist
verifies: The exclusion needs a family home that was the parent's principal residence and becomes the child's
Value limit: current taxable value plus $1,000,000 (adjusted every two years)
Homeowners' exemption within 1 year; exclusion claim within 3 years or before a sale to a third party
A rental home does not qualify
If the child later moves out, the home is taxed on its market value at the date of inheritance, factored forward
For a trust, the date of death is the date of change in ownership
boe_prop19.quote: No, Proposition 19 limits the parent-child transfer exclusion to a transfer of (1) a family home that is the principal residence of the transferor and becomes the principal residence of the transferee, or (2) a family farm. Thus, the transfer of a rental home between parents and children would not qualify for the exclusion.

Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,044,586.

boe_lta26026.title: Letter to Assessors 2026/026: intergenerational transfer exclusion questions and answers (3 Aug 2026)
verifies: In a multi-unit building only the unit occupied as the parent's principal residence can qualify; the rest is reassessed at full cash value (Q5, Q15)
Property held through an LLC, even a single-member LLC, is not eligible (Q32-Q35)
A transfer through a trust qualifies if the statute's conditions are met (Q39)
A trustee with power to distribute non-pro-rata can give the home to one child without a sibling-to-sibling reassessment (Q41-Q42)

boe_lta26026.quote: No, only the unit occupied as the principal residence qualifies as the principal residence of the transferor. The remainder of the apartment complex would be ineligible for the intergenerational transfer exclusion and would be reassessed at its full cash value as of the date of transfer.
